extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, historians of mathematics, and advanced students studying classical geometry (Archimedes)
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of definitions, lemmas, constructions and propositions from Archimedes' treatises 'Measurement of a Circle' and 'On Conoids and Spheroids' focusing on statements, constructions and proportional relationships used in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of exhaustion via inscribed/circumscribed polygons (area of a circle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show the area of a circle equals a given magnitude K by constructing inscribed and circumscribed polygons whose areas bracket the circle and whose excess/defect can be made smaller than any prescribed quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circumscribe polygons, bisect arcs and draw tangents at midpoints to produce polygons approximating the circle; by making the polygon sufficiently fine the total area between polygon and circle becomes less than any given excess. Use comparison of perpendiculars from center to sides (equal to radius) and relations between polygon perimeter and circumference to derive contradictions if assumed area differs from K. (Full stepwise construction and contradiction argument given.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: area of a circle proportional to square on its diameter (archival statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of a circle is to the square on its diameter as 11 to 14. (Text notes this statement in the source is unsatisfactory and depends on later approximations.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes' original text places this proposition before Proposition 3 though its derivation depends on the approximations obtained later; the translator/editorial note warns that intermediate steps are often omitted in the Greek text and some approximations are merely stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounds for circumference-to-diameter ratio (pi bounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio of the circumference of any circle to its diameter is less than 22/7 but greater than 223/71. (Rendered in the text as 'less than 34 but greater than 3}9' with accompanying construction.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes obtains the bounds by constructing regular inscribed and circumscribed polygons (here a regular polygon with 96 sides is used) via successive angle bisections of one-third of a right angle and computing (or stating) numerical inequalities for side ratios; the text encloses many intermediate steps (often supplied by Eutocius) in brackets and notes that some square-root and fractional approximations are asserted without full arithmetic detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction technique: successive angle bisection to construct high-sided regular polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: Bisect an angle repeatedly (here four times) to divide one-third of a right angle into 1/48 (and correspondingly construct a 96-sided polygon) to produce sides of regular inscribed/circumscribed polygons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use angle bisectors from the center to obtain chord/side lengths and compare OA:AG and related ratios; double lengths of chord segments to relate to polygon side lengths (e.g., GH = 2*AG) and infer perimeter bounds for the circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: right-angled conoid (paraboloid of revolution) and segment
rubrics_metrics.description: A right-angled conoid is the solid obtained by revolving a section of a right-angled cone (a parabola) about the diameter (axis) which remains fixed. The axis is the fixed diameter, vertex is where axis meets the surface; if a plane tangent and a plane parallel to the tangent cut off a segment, the base is the section on the cutting plane, vertex is the tangent point, and axis of the segment is the portion cut off from the line through the vertex parallel to the conoid axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology is set to preserve Archimedes' Greek terms; subsequent propositions use these definitions to compare segments with cones and to show proportionality relations between segments' axes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: obtuse-angled conoid (hyperboloid of revolution), enveloping cone, adjacent line
rubrics_metrics.description: An obtuse-angled conoid arises from revolving a section of an obtuse-angled cone (a hyperbola) about its diameter (axis). The nearest lines to the section (asymptotes) generate an isosceles enveloping cone whose vertex is at their intersection; the straight line joining the conoid vertex and vertex of enveloping cone is called adjacent to the axis. Definitions of base, vertex and axis of segments mirror the right-angled case but use the enveloping cone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Right-angled conoids are all similar; obtuse-angled conoids are considered similar when their enveloping cones are similar. Propositions state ratios of segments to cones involving sums of the axis and multiples of the adjacent line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: spheroidal figures (oblong and flat spheroids) and related terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: If an acute-angled cone (an ellipse) is revolved about its major diameter (axis) an oblong spheroid results; about its minor diameter a flat spheroid results. Axis is the fixed diameter; vertex is where axis meets surface; centre is middle of axis; diameter is line through centre perpendicular to axis. Definitions of bases, vertices and axes for segments follow from parallel tangent planes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties to be proved: tangent planes meet spheroid at one point; line joining tangent points passes through centre. Similarity criteria: spheroids are similar when axes have same ratio to diameters; segments are similar if cut from similar figures with similar bases and axes in same relation to bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problems posed for conoids and spheroids (overview of intended theorems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes lists exact questions to be addressed: for conoids, ratios between segments and cones involving axis and adjacent line; for spheroids, ratios between segments and cones/cylinders/spheres in various cutting-plane configurations (through centre or not, at right angles or not), and triplicate proportionality results for similar figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These problem statements set the objectives of the treatise and determine which auxiliary lemmas and constructions will be developed first. Several corollaries and applied problems (e.g., cutting off a segment equal to a given cone/cylinder/sphere) are announced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: inequalities for ascending arithmetic progression
rubrics_metrics.description: If A1, A2, ... , An form an ascending arithmetic progression whose common difference equals the least term A1, then n*A_n < 2(A1 + A2 + ... + An) and n*A1 > 2(A1 + A2 + ... + A_{n-1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes gives a geometric (line-placing) proof by juxtaposing terms and producing earlier terms to equal the greatest term; he uses these inequalities in later summation and area arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 1 (ratio-preserving sums): equality of compounded sums under proportion hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two series A1, B1, C1, ... and A2, B2, C2, ... with pairwise proportionalities (A1:A2 = B1:B2 = ... ) and similarly two other series obeying analogous proportionalities, then the ratio of sums (A1+B1+...):(A2+B2+...) equals the ratio of the alternate sums (A1'+B1'+...):(A2'+B2'+...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses ex aequali argument and repeated application of pairwise proportionalities; a corollary states the result still holds if corresponding last terms are omitted. This proposition is a tool for combining proportional relationships into ratios of total sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma to Proposition 2: sum-of-squares identity for arithmetic progression
rubrics_metrics.description: For an ascending arithmetic progression A1, A2, ... , An where the common difference equals the least term A1, an identity relates (n+1)A_n^2 + A1(A1 + ... + An) to 3(sum of squares A1^2 + ... + An^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes proves this by geometric rearrangement (producing terms to match the greatest term) and algebraic grouping; several corollaries about bounds on sums and inequalities of sums of squares are derived and later applied to area comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 2: inequalities for areas composed from applied rectangles (application of areas method)
rubrics_metrics.description: If areas A1, A2, ..., An are constructed by applying rectangles exceeding by squares with parameters given (Ai = a * i^x + (i x)^2 etc.), then inequalities relate n*An and sums of Ai to expressions depending on a, n and their parameters (precise inequalities given in terms of a, n, x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes uses the preceding lemma and the method of application of areas (applying rectangles exceeding by a square) to derive bounds on total areas and to compare sums of such constructed areas to sums of squares. The proposition is technical and used in geometric-analytic arguments later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3(1): tangent-chord ratio theorem for conics
rubrics_metrics.description: If TP and TP' are two tangents to any conic meeting at T, and QQ and Q'Q' are two chords parallel to TP and TP' meeting at O, then QO·Oq : Q'0·0q' = TP^2 : TP'^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes refers to existing elements of conics (Aristaeus / Euclid) for proof; the result relates tangent lengths at an external point to products of chord segments determined by parallels through an internal point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3(2): constancy of triangle and segment area for parabola
rubrics_metrics.description: For a parabola, if QQ' is a chord bisected in V by diameter PV and PV is fixed in length, then the area of triangle PQQ' and the area of the segment PQQ' are both constant regardless of the chord direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to equalities of products of ordinate parameters: QV^2 = p·PV where p is parameter of the principal ordinates; relationships BH^2 = p·AH etc. The segment area equals 4 times the triangle area by known quadrature relations of the parabola (references to Quadrature of the Parabola).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 4: area of an ellipse proportional to auxiliary circle by minor:major axis
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of any ellipse is to that of its auxiliary circle as the minor axis is to the major axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: assume auxiliary circle area greater or less than ellipse, inscribe polygons in circle and ellipse with same number of sides and show proportionality of perpendiculars yields polygon area ratios equal to CA:CB (major:minor), leading to contradiction. Uses polygon approximation technique similar to circle area arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 5 & 6: area relations of ellipses (rectangles under axes and circle comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prop.5: (area of ellipse):(area of any circle of diameter d) = AA'·BB' : d^2. Prop.6: Areas of ellipses are proportional to the rectangles under their axes; corollary: areas of similar ellipses are as squares of corresponding linear measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 5 follows from Prop.4 (ellipse:auxiliary circle :: minor:major) and area scaling for circles; Prop.6 follows immediately. These are structural area-ratio rules used in later constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 7: construction of cone through an ellipse with given external vertex
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an ellipse with centre C and a line CO perpendicular to its plane, it is possible to find a circular cone with vertex O whose surface passes through the entire circumference of the ellipse (i.e., ellipse is a section of that cone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct BD as a diameter in a perpendicular plane and choose BE, ED so that BE·ED : EO^2 = CA^2 : CO^2; form the cone on BD as base and vertex O; for any point P on the ellipse, produce perpendiculars and similar-triangle arguments to show P lies on the cone surface (establishing straightness of OPQ). Uses product-of-segments equalities and right-triangle properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 8: construction of cone through ellipse when vertex plane contains axis but not perpendicular
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an ellipse and a plane through one axis AA' but not perpendicular to it and a line CO in that plane, one can find a cone with vertex O whose surface contains the ellipse (again, the ellipse is a conical section).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: produce OA' to D so that VA = OD, draw AD, construct an auxiliary circle or ellipse on AD depending on a proportion condition, then choose a cone through that auxiliary curve with vertex O. For any point P on the ellipse, use perpendiculars and segment-product identities to show P lies on the cone's generator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 9: construction of cylinder through ellipse with given axis OC (three cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an ellipse, a plane through one axis AA' and a line CO in that plane (not perpendicular to AA'), it is possible to find a cylinder with axis OC whose surface passes through the ellipse. Three cases depend on the relation between BB' (the other axis) and DE (constructed line): (1) BB' = DE, (2) BB' > DE, (3) BB' < DE, with corresponding constructions (circle on appropriate diameter or auxiliary construction with added perpendicular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In each case draw perpendiculars from ellipse points, construct an auxiliary circle in a plane perpendicular to OC with appropriate diameter, and show via segment-product equalities that for any point P on the ellipse the corresponding PQ is parallel to OC so PQ is a cylinder generator. Detailed trigonometric/similarity relations are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 10: ratios of cones and frustums; frustum is triple conical segment
rubrics_metrics.description: Any two cones have to one another the ratio compounded of the ratios of their bases and of their heights; similarly any segments of cones have their ratio compounded of ratios of bases and heights. Also, any frustum of a cylinder is triple of the conical segment having the same base and equal height (analogy to cylinder triple-of-cone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes indicates these results follow from Euclid XII propositions and earlier methods used for cylinder-cone volume relations; proof method is the same as for showing cylinder is triple of cone of same base and height.
